clue.text: Serious crime — using criminal's money?

parts.note: the money a person or a business has to work with
the possessive ending says the money belongs to him, and belonging to is of
a fence is the crook who buys stolen goods from thieves and sells them on

explanation.surface: A grave crime paid for out of a crook's own funds.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital does double work — the sense that used to hang a man in the definition, the sense that sits in a bank account in the wordplay. The spaces of the answer fall nowhere near the joins of the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: A capital offence is one the law once punished by death, which makes it the gravest sort of serious crime.

clue.text: Arrives clutching a gift, but a fancy soldier's attire

indicators.note: To clutch a thing is to close your grip right round it, so what follows is shut inside the word in front rather than set beside it.

parts.note: somebody who arrives comes, the verb in the same third-person form

indicators.note: Something fancy has been worked up out of its plain state, and letters worked up like that do not stay in the order they were handed over in.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder, three little words taken straight off the page

explanation.surface: A visitor turns up hugging a present, but is dressed in something rather grand for a soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'gift' is the setter's, not the sentence's: 'but a' belongs to the letters being shuffled, not to the objection the surface seems to be raising. Fatigues are a soldier's plain working dress, the opposite of fancy.
explanation.definitionFit: Combat fatigues are the hard-wearing camouflage kit a soldier works and fights in, so the definition names them by who wears them.

clue.text: After start of play, suggest getting spots

indicators.note: What comes after a thing is written behind it, so the single letter taken here stands at the front and the longer word trails it.
The start of a word is where it begins, so only its opening letter is wanted.

parts.note: the letter the word begins with
to imply something is to suggest it without ever saying it

explanation.surface: Once play has started, somebody proposes going out to get spots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start of play' is the cricket commentator's phrase for the first ball of the day, which is why it reads as a time of morning rather than as an instruction about a letter. The spots wanted are the teenage sort.
explanation.definitionFit: Pimply is the adjective for skin breaking out in pimples, which are exactly the spots a face collects.

clue.text: Dismissed report from start to finish

indicators.note: A report is what somebody said passed on by ear, so the words beside it are wanted as they sound and not as they are spelt.

parts.note: a man dismissed from his job has been thrown out, and that pair of words said aloud is spelt quite differently

explanation.surface: An account of somebody's sacking, followed from beginning to end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From start to finish' looks like an instruction to take letters off the ends of things; it is the definition. 'Dismissed' has to shift from adjective to past-tense verb before it sounds like anything at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that goes on throughout goes on for the whole span of whatever is being talked about, which is the stretch from start to finish.

clue.text: Some terribly cramped cycling gear

indicators.note: Some of a thing is a part of it, and the part wanted here is a run of letters lifted straight out of the words that follow.

parts.note: five consecutive letters running across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: Cycling kit so tight that the wearer looks terribly cramped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terribly' works hard as an adverb in the surface, so the eye reads it instead of looking at it, and the run straddles the word break. Lycra is the stretch fabric cycling shorts are made of.
explanation.definitionFit: Lycra is the elastic fabric cycling shorts and jerseys are made from, so the definition names the material by the kit it turns into.

clue.text: See 1
Their responsibility to send one back to France is being served

indicators.note: Something sent back travels the way it came, so the word it points at is written from its last letter to its first.
A word sent to France is wanted in French, so 'one' is taken in that language rather than in English.

parts.note: if a job is on them, it is theirs to see to
the French for one is une, taken the other way round

explanation.surface: Sending a man home to France is somebody else's job, and dinner is being served.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's on them' is the idiom the long piece comes from, and the spaces in the answer fall nowhere near the joins in the wordplay. A restaurant is nowhere in the surface, which is all diplomacy and deportation.
explanation.definitionFit: A dish on the menu is one the kitchen is offering that day, so the phrase says what is being served without naming any of it.

clue.text: Overweight and eating lettuce? At last, an achievement!

indicators.note: What is eaten goes inside the eater, so the letter taken next sits within the word in front of it.

parts.note: somebody overweight is fat, the plain three-letter word for it

indicators.note: At last means at the very end, so only the final letter of the word before it is taken.

parts.note: the letter the word ends on

explanation.surface: A heavy eater has finally got round to some salad, which is quite something.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and the exclamation both belong to the surface's little scene of a reluctant dieter, and they cover the fact that 'At last' is an instruction rather than a sigh of relief.
explanation.definitionFit: A feat is a difficult thing somebody has pulled off, which is what calling it an achievement says.

clue.text: Legal workers ignoring those born in March or April

parts.note: to ignore a thing is to carry on as though it were not there, and 'not' is the word that rules it out

parts.words: those born in March or April
parts.note: the zodiac sign that runs from late March into April is Aries, the ram

explanation.surface: Lawyers who will not deal with anybody whose birthday falls in early spring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ignoring' reads as a snobbish refusal and is a flat instruction to write the word that cancels. Aries covers birthdays from 21 March to 19 April, which is what makes the two months a fair way of naming it.
explanation.definitionFit: A notary is an official who witnesses signatures and certifies documents, so 'legal workers' names the job by the trade it sits in.

clue.text: Raise special case after hours

indicators.note: Something special is out of the ordinary, and letters taken out of their ordinary order have to be written in a new one.

parts.note: four letters of fodder, the word taken as it stands
something done after hours is done late

explanation.surface: Bringing up an unusual case once the office has shut for the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Special case' is such a fixed phrase that the two words look welded together, and only one of them is fodder. 'After hours' hands over a whole piece rather than telling you where a piece goes.
explanation.definitionFit: To escalate a complaint is to raise it to a higher level, which is the sense of 'raise' the clue is after.

clue.text: Note musical entertainment role to begin with silent performer

parts.note: mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale singers count up

indicators.note: To begin with points at where words start, so the opening letter of each of the three in front is taken and nothing else.

parts.note: the opening letters of the three words, in the order they are given

explanation.surface: Jotting down the entertainment role in a musical, starting with the turn nobody can hear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' opens the clue looking like an imperative — notice this — and is a noun handing over two letters. 'To begin with' then has to reach back across all three of the words in front of it, not just one.
explanation.definitionFit: A mimer performs in mime, telling the story with gesture alone, so 'silent performer' names the act by the one thing it never uses.

clue.text: Purging most of the Arctic a muddle

indicators.note: Most of a word is not all of it, so the word it points at arrives one letter short of its full spelling.
Things in a muddle are not in the order they were left in, and nor are these letters.

parts.note: the three-letter word docked of its last letter
seven more letters of fodder, taken as they stand

explanation.surface: Clearing out most of the Arctic and leaving a muddle behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of the' looks as though it is heading for 'most of the Arctic' and stops a word earlier: it is the little word that gets docked. A cathartic, in medicine, is a drug that empties the bowels.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathartic purges the system, and the same word covers the emotional clear-out a tragedy is meant to give its audience.

clue.text: Overwhelming majority expressed relief after everyone played tuba

indicators.note: Something expressed has been said out loud, so the word beside it is wanted as the ear takes it rather than as the page spells it.

parts.note: everyone there is all of them

indicators.note: What comes after everything else is written last, so the piece the clue names first is the one that ends up at the end.
To play an instrument is to sound its notes in whatever order the music asks, so the letters beside it are free to move.

parts.note: four letters of fodder, the brass instrument itself
the noise you let out when relief arrives is phew, and said aloud it is written another way

explanation.surface: Everybody sighing with relief once the tuba player has finally stopped.
explanation.walkthrough: The relief goes in where it is heard rather than where it is spelt, and 'after' sends it to the back of the answer even though the clue names it first. Phew and its homophone differ by a single silent letter.
explanation.definitionFit: All but a few means everyone bar a handful, and a handful against everyone else is what makes a majority overwhelming.

clue.text: Your fault every now and then, to get mouthy?

indicators.note: Something done every now and then is done at intervals rather than all the way through, so the letters are picked up at every second step.

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of the two words read together

explanation.surface: Being told the blame is yours, at least some of the time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mouthy' means cheeky in the surface and of the mouth in the definition, a sense the word does not really carry off the crossword page — the question mark is the setter owning up to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Oral means done by mouth, as in an oral exam or an oral dose, and 'mouthy' is the setter's cheeky adjective for exactly that.

clue.text: Like people around one, they can be cast

parts.note: like a lion = as a lion, the two swapping freely in a comparison

indicators.note: What goes around a thing encloses it, so the letter named next sits inside the word before it.

parts.note: persons is the stiffer plural of person, the one legal English prefers
one in Roman numerals is the single upright stroke

explanation.surface: A crowd pressing round a single figure, and something that gets thrown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' wants to be a theatre company or a plaster one, and is the verb that goes with this noun and almost no other. 'Persons' rather than 'people' is where the S comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspersions are damaging insinuations, and English throws them with one verb only: you cast aspersions, and cast very little else of the kind.

clue.text: Straight coverage of outrageous rents in a difficult situation

indicators.note: Coverage of a thing is what lies over it, so the word in front opens up and wraps round the letters that follow.

parts.note: a straight dealer is an honest one

indicators.note: What is outrageous has gone beyond its proper bounds, and letters beyond their proper places have to be rewritten.

parts.note: five letters of fodder, the word as the landlord writes it

explanation.surface: Even-handed news coverage of scandalous rents, filed from somewhere awkward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coverage' belongs to the newsroom in the surface and to the wrapping in the wordplay. The 'in' before the definition looks like an insertion instruction and is only joining the two halves of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To stir up a hornet's nest is to land in trouble coming at you from every side, so the phrase names a difficult situation by its liveliest example.

clue.text: Lying about wobbly bum is modern

indicators.note: What is placed about a thing is wrapped round it, so the word named at the end of the clue closes over the letters in the middle.

parts.note: recent events are the modern ones, the things that have just happened

indicators.note: Something wobbly will not hold still, and letters that will not hold still cannot be left in the order they came in.

parts.note: three letters of fodder, the backside of the surface

explanation.surface: Telling untruths about somebody's wobbly backside is apparently the modern way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lying' is the definition and reads in the surface as telling untruths, while the answer means lying down. 'About' is doing an insertion here rather than meaning 'concerning', which is the other thing the surface wants it to be.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody recumbent is lying down, stretched out on a couch or a bed, so participle and adjective describe the same posture.

clue.text: See 1
Total reversal on trainee making wine

indicators.note: A reversal turns a word end for end, so the word before it goes into the grid from its last letter to its first.
In a down clue whatever sits on something else stands above it, so the piece named first is written in at the top.

parts.note: a total is a sum, here written end for end
a cadet is a trainee in the forces or the police

explanation.surface: A complete about-turn in policy concerning a trainee winemaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Total reversal' is one phrase in the surface and two separate instructions in the wordplay: the noun first, then what to do with it. Muscadet is the dry white made near the mouth of the Loire.
explanation.definitionFit: Muscadet is the crisp dry white pressed from melon de Bourgogne grapes around Nantes, so 'wine' names it by its kind.

clue.text: Point in time when Juliet left after a prize for needlework

indicators.note: What has left is no longer where it was, so the letter named beside it goes missing from the word it was sitting in.
What comes after something is written behind it, so the long piece follows the two short ones even though the clue names it first.

parts.note: the indefinite article, taken as it stands
the cup is the prize a winning captain lifts
a juncture is a point in time, and it has lost a letter from the front — the next block says which
Juliet is J in the radio alphabet police and pilots spell with

explanation.surface: The moment Juliet walked out, just after she had won a prize for her sewing.
explanation.walkthrough: Juliet is the radio alphabet's J rather than Shakespeare's heroine, though the surface would much rather you thought about the balcony. 'Needlework' is the joke of the clue and is also literally true of the treatment.
explanation.definitionFit: Acupuncture is treatment by pushing fine needles into the body, so calling it needlework is a straight-faced description as well as a gag.

clue.text: Articles about booze causing pain

indicators.note: What is set about a thing is wrapped round it, so the letters in front close over the word that follows.

parts.note: two of the indefinite articles, an and then a
gin, the juniper spirit, is the booze here

explanation.surface: Newspaper pieces about drink and the harm it does.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' reads as newspaper pieces and means the grammatical sort, of which the clue needs two rather than one. Angina is the gripping chest pain of a heart muscle short of blood.
explanation.definitionFit: Angina is the tight chest pain that comes when the heart is starved of blood, so 'pain' names it by what the patient actually feels.

clue.text: Value committee finally meets up

indicators.note: In a down clue letters written up the grid are read from the bottom, so the word before it goes in backwards.
Finally means at the very end, so only the last letter of the word in front of it is taken.

parts.note: the letter the long word ends on
the five letters climbing back up the grid

explanation.surface: After all this time, the valuation committee is finally getting together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meets up' is one phrasal verb in the surface and two separate things in the wordplay, the second of them an instruction about direction. 'Finally' points at the letter a word ends on, not at the last item in a list.
explanation.definitionFit: To esteem something is to value it, both verbs meaning to reckon it worth a great deal.

clue.text: Desire to get some kitchenware

indicators.note: Some of a thing is a part of it, so a part of the word that follows is taken out whole.

parts.note: four letters sitting side by side inside the longer word

explanation.surface: Fancying a few new pots and pans.
explanation.walkthrough: The hiding place is one word rather than a run across a gap, so there is no join to give it away. 'Kitchenware' is long enough and dull enough that the eye slides straight over it.
explanation.definitionFit: An itch for something is a restless craving you cannot leave alone, which is desire of the nagging kind.

clue.text: They're held by Bonnie & Clyde and Butch Cassidy & the Sundance Kid before noon, each case for sheriffs

definitions.text: They're held by Bonnie & Clyde and Butch Cassidy & the Sundance Kid

indicators.note: The case of a thing is the shell it comes in, so what is wanted is the pair of letters at either end of the word that follows.

parts.note: AM is ante meridiem, the hours before midday
per head means each head, so per is each
the letters at either end of the word are both S, and saying that pair out in full is what puts the joining word between them

explanation.surface: Two outlaw double acts rounded up before midday, with a case each for the sheriffs.
explanation.walkthrough: Two ampersands are sitting in the clue in plain sight, holding the famous pairs together. The last piece is an instruction written out as speech: the outer letters of 'sheriffs', which you read off as S and S.
explanation.definitionFit: Both outlaw pairs are billed with & joining the names, and that symbol is an ampersand, so the clue's own text is holding two of them.

clue.text: Sandwich-like ahead of time?

parts.note: the Earl of Sandwich is the nobleman the snack is named for, Sandwich itself being a town in Kent
the ending -y is what English adds to a noun to mean like that thing, as in chalky or silky

explanation.surface: A snack rather like a sandwich, arriving before anybody expected it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwich-like' reads as one adjective and the hyphen is what hides the join. The Earl of Sandwich is the eighteenth-century peer who had his meat served between bread so he need not leave the card table.
explanation.definitionFit: Early is the plain word for anything happening sooner than the clock said it would, which is what being ahead of time amounts to.

clue.text: Press club

definitions.meaning: the verb for flattening a shirt with a hot flat thing
the golfer's metal-headed stick, numbered from three upwards

explanation.surface: The press club, where journalists gather.
explanation.walkthrough: A press club is a real institution, a journalists' association, and reading the two words as one phrase is the whole trap. The club wanted is the golfer's, the metal-headed sort rather than the wooden one.
explanation.definitionFit: To iron a shirt is to press it flat with heat, and an iron is also the club a golfer takes for a mid-range shot.

clue.text: Like Bishop Auckland's pants?

definitions.note: Pants is a plural-only noun and the answer a mass noun taking a singular verb; neither can be counted and both name the same garments, which is why the swap works in a sentence but not in the grammar.

parts.note: the County Durham town stands on the south bank, which puts it below the river beside it
that river, which runs on through Durham to the sea, is the Wear

explanation.surface: Asking whether something is like the underpants belonging to the Bishop of Auckland.
explanation.walkthrough: Bishop Auckland is a town in County Durham rather than a churchman, and it is the one piece of British geography the puzzle asks you to know. In British usage pants are worn under everything else, not instead of trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain pants are the undergarments worn next to the skin rather than trousers, so the word names exactly the clothing the answer covers.

clue.text: Surmise long after love

indicators.note: What comes after a thing is written behind it, so the longer piece follows the letter even though the clue names it first.

parts.note: love is a score of nothing in tennis, written as the round letter
to pine for somebody is to long for them

explanation.surface: Working out, long after the affair ended, what must have been going on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long after love' reads as a stretch of time and is two separate pieces, with 'long' the verb meaning to yearn. Love for nothing comes from the tennis scoreboard.
explanation.definitionFit: To opine is to venture an opinion rather than a fact, which is what surmising sounds like when it is said out loud.

clue.text: Put off deciding what to do with a chair

definitions.meaning: the committee's way of shelving a report without ever refusing it

definitions.text: what to do with a chair
definitions.meaning: the plain physical instruction, taken absolutely literally

explanation.surface: Postponing any decision about what should happen to a chair.
explanation.walkthrough: The two definitions share the middle of the sentence, so the clue reads as one thought about an awkward piece of furniture rather than as two. Sitting on a report is what a committee does to bury it.
explanation.definitionFit: To sit on a decision is to leave it unmade; a chair is the thing you literally sit on, so the phrase works at both levels.

clue.text: Same problem in root whatever you say

indicators.note: A word called a problem is a word in trouble, and letters in trouble are no longer standing in the order they were given.

parts.note: the yam is the root vegetable, a staple across west Africa and the Caribbean

indicators.note: Something in a thing sits inside it, so the letters named before this word go within the word after it.

parts.note: four letters of fodder, the word as the clue opens with it

explanation.surface: The same trouble turning up down among the roots, whatever anybody tells you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Root' pulls towards a tooth or a square root and is the vegetable. The split leaves just one letter of it in front, which is why the join is so hard to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Yes ma'am' is the reply of somebody who will agree to anything an officer or an employer asks, which is 'whatever you say' said smartly.
